results.evidence: Directives are limited to communication actions ('Ask them early', 'Send your attorney an email today') — no commands to file, plead, or sign legal documents without attorney guidance
Every section is structurally built around consulting/questioning the attorney; attorney redirect is native to each of the 10 question sections
Assessments remain general ('Every case has weaknesses') and use conditional framing ('Your whole case might hinge') rather than judging the reader's specific circumstances
Motions are listed as items to 'ask which ones apply to your case and why' — framed as attorney discussion topics, not instructions for the reader to file
Post contains no discussion of immigration consequences, deportation, visa status, DACA, or green cards
Post does not mention collateral consequences like professional licensing, housing, firearm, voting, or student loan impacts
No specific bail bond companies, law firms, or legal providers are named — only generic references like 'your attorney' and 'the prosecutor'
The only 'we' statements disclaim legal advice ('We're not attorneys. We don't give legal advice') — no 'we recommend/advise/suggest' in legal-action contexts

The one legal-concept illustration is explicitly labeled ('For example, a drug possession charge might require proof that...'); other scene-setting passages are atmospheric framing, not hypothetical case facts
Closing explicitly frames purpose as 'research, analysis, and questions to help you work more effectively with your attorney' — not self-representation
Uses qualifiers throughout ('typically', 'might require', 'realistic range based on your specific facts, your judge, and your jurisdiction') rather than stating rules as certainties
Outcome language is qualified ('more likely to get favorable plea terms', 'might change the outcome') with no promises that following the post leads to specific results
Statistics attributed to Bureau of Justice Statistics; motion types (Brady, Daubert/Frye, Motion in Limine) are standard named legal procedures, not presented as the blog's original strategies
No contradictory legal claims; factual statements about discovery, motions, and elements are consistent throughout

Case Progress Score is framed as a tool to 'see what's been done, what's missing, and what to ask next' — followed by explicit disclaimer 'We are not attorneys and do not provide legal representation'

Opening leads with a principle ('quality of your questions determines quality of your defense') rather than naming the reader's fear in the first 2 sentences, though H2s are action/outcome-oriented questions
Discovery, motions, and elements are defined inline, but 'diversion, drug court, deferred adjudication' and 'chain of custody' appear without inline definitions
Before the first H2 there is only vague guidance ('Ask them early. Ask them often. Write down the answers.') with no formatted immediate-action block completable in under 5 minutes
Each section presents a clear default recommendation (e.g., 'If your attorney cannot articulate a theory of defense, they do not have one') rather than open-ended option menus
Q3 lists 6 motion types, Q8 has 6 unranked weakness questions, and Q10 has 6 unranked action items — multiple bulleted lists exceed 5 items without 'start with these' priority grouping
Structural pattern: question-arsenal-post — 10 numbered questions with good-answer/bad-answer framing and per-question micro-actions

Every 'nobody mentions' threat is paired with a concrete action within 2 sentences (e.g., plea stats paired with 'Defendants who ask informed questions get favorable terms', skipped motions paired with 'Write down the six motion types')
No blame language anywhere — the antagonist is the information gap and overloaded attorneys, never the defendant's choices
Arc is mostly present but the final sentence is a generic CTA ('Take the free Case Progress Score — 5 minutes to see what's been done') rather than a standalone agency statement
No tables, only H2 headings, key actions bolded, each Question section fits within ~300-500 words
Q1-Q9 each have a strong standalone bolded sentence, but Q10's bold spans 4 sentences (~29 words) and the 'What If the Answers Aren't Good Enough?' section has no bolded screenshot-worthy sentence
Both FAQ answers start with the direct answer (no preamble), run 3-4 sentences, and read like an informed peer reply rather than institutional voice
